short.thema: McDonald's: the brothers who cut 20 carhops and later sold their stake
short.text:
They fired all 20 carhops and ditched every plate. McDonald's brothers sold out. Why?

Richard and Maurice McDonald opened in California in 1940, chasing $1 million before turning 50.

In 1948, paper replaced plates and silverware. The menu shrank to nine items.

Ray Kroc became a McDonald's franchise agent in 1955. Who would win control?

They fought for control. In 1961, Kroc bought their stake for $2.7 million.

No carhops, no plates, no brothers. McDonald's had 45,356 restaurants by 2025's end.

lang.thema: GTA V radio: 441 licensed tracks - how a game became a giant radio platform
lang.titel: GTA V's 441 Tracks: How a Game Became a Radio
lang.text:
He rejected the offer at first. Tangerine Dream's founder didn't want to make music for Grand Theft Auto V. Yet that game now has a radio carrying more than 441 licensed tracks. And the reason he changed his mind comes later.

This video answers one question. How did Grand Theft Auto V turn licensed music into a giant radio world, and what did its original score do beside it?

The game's in-game radio shares its tracks between 18 stations, including two talk radio stations. Together they play more than 441 tracks of licensed music. Rockstar North developed the game, and Rockstar Games published it.

The stations span reggae, hip hop, hardcore punk, pop and country. How do you make each one feel like a place? The team licensed tracks they felt echoed a Cali feel. Then they picked a DJ to match each station's genre.

Los Santos Rock Radio got classic rock tracks. The team decided Kenny Loggins was a fitting DJ for it. Be sure to like, share and save this video.

Rockstar first planned to license over 900 tracks. Over time, the team refined that total. Place mattered. The game is modelled on Southern California, and the developers wanted an accurate picture of the region.

Pavlovich recalled the first time you get off an airplane in L.A. and hear the radio. The pop just seeps out, he said. The team wanted that, because it connects you to the world.

Some tracks were written for the game itself. Rapper and producer Flying Lotus hosts the station FlyLo FM, which includes original work he composed for it.

Pavlovich said licensing here took greater discernment than in Grand Theft Auto IV. The music played a bigger role in building a Californian atmosphere. It reflects the environment in which the game is set, he explained.

PC players got something extra. Self Radio is a customizable station where users include their favorite tunes. The Windows version, released on 14 April 2015, also shipped an album for a fictional station called The Lab.

That album, from The Alchemist and Oh No, was put on The Lab to fit the rest of the in-game music. AllMusic's David Jeffries felt it captures the excitement of flipping the radio dial in the game. NPR's Andrew Matson thought some tracks were unconsidered.

But the radio wasn't the only music. Unlike most predecessors, this game also used an original score. Pavlovich called the idea daunting, because it was unprecedented for a Grand Theft Auto game.

He hoped the score would enhance the licensed music, not detract from it. The balancing act was between its ambient subtext and tensions and the onscreen action.

Rockstar engaged The Alchemist, Oh No, Tangerine Dream and Woody Jackson. Jackson had worked on Red Dead Redemption, L.A. Noire and Max Payne 3. Over several years, the team produced more than twenty hours of music.

Now back to the founder who said no. Edgar Froese initially rejected the offer of producing music for a video game. Then Rockstar flew him to the studio and showed him the game. He was impressed by its scale and cinematic nature, and changed his mind.

He was also intrigued by the game's philosophy of working against the establishment, despite his distaste for the medium. He described it as a social game.

His first eight months of work produced 62 hours of music. He recorded with Tangerine Dream in Austria. More work happened at Jackson's studio in the United States, which The Alchemist and Oh No used too.

Then came a worry. Jackson began with score for Trevor's missions. When he learned the team would build on each other's work, he feared the finished product could sound disjointed.

Then they shared the work. Jackson was particularly impressed by Froese. Edgar evolved the music, made it into a whole other thing, he said. Froese had interpolated funk sounds with Jackson's hip-hop influences.

Froese and Jackson sent their work between The Alchemist and Oh No, who heavily sampled it. We pitched stuff up, chopped it, tweaked it, The Alchemist said. Then everyone layered on top of the tracks that worked.

DJ Shadow then mixed the team's creations together and matched them to the gameplay. Pavlovich saw one challenge: the hip-hop and rock score shouldn't sound like instrumentals of songs on the radio. It had to be something unique to the score.

Players make unpredictable choices, so the team used a stem-based system. They composed music to underscore outcomes players could cause right after completing missions.

Froese reflected that each stem included up to 62 five-minute WAV files, sent to Pavlovich in New York. Pavlovich created a mix down for each of the eight stems needed for a mission and sent the material to the other artists.

Oh No drew on scenes in the game. Its iconic introduction of Los Santos inspired him to create a smooth West Coast vibe. For car chases, he supplied horns, electric and bass guitars, and percussion.

The work ran right to the end. The team started after seeing an early build, and kept composing until the final build was submitted for manufacturing. Some random creations even sparked other missions.

Then the music left the game. The Music of Grand Theft Auto V arrived digitally on 24 September 2013, in three volumes of score and radio selections. It peaked at 11 on Billboard's Top Soundtracks chart.

Froese's own album, The Cinematographic Score, came out in March 2014, limited to 2000 copies. A retail version of the main soundtrack followed on 9 December 2014, on CD and vinyl.

Online kept adding music. Health released an Arena War album on 1 March 2019. Three singles arrived with The Cayo Perico Heist update on 18 December 2020. DāM-FunK's collection followed on 15 December 2023.

New Dr. Dre music reached Grand Theft Auto Online in December 2021, and a digital EP followed in February 2022. For the base game, it was announced in September 2014 that new songs would be added to some stations in next-gen releases.

Critics largely approved. Edge wrote that the licensed music enriches Los Santos' remarkable sense of space. GameSpot's Carolyn Petit said the score lends missions more cinematic flavour. Giant Bomb's Jeff Gerstmann said it helped enhance dramatic tension.

IGN's Keza MacDonald thought the licensed music was selected well. The Guardian's Tshepo Mokoena called the soundtrack inaccessibly trendy at points, but varied enough.

So how did a game become a giant radio platform? Rockstar planned over 900 tracks, then refined the total. It built stations around place, genre and the right DJ, ending up with more than 441 licensed tracks across 18 stations, including two talk stations. Beside them sat an original score of more than twenty hours, meant to accompany the licensed music, not detract from it. And the founder who first rejected the offer agreed to work on it once he saw the game's scale. Be sure to like, share and save this video.
